# No Voltage on Injector Lines Following Engine Rebuild

When you rebuild an engine, it is tempting to assume that if the mechanical assembly was done correctly, the electronics will just "magically" reconnect once the bolts are torqued. However, fuel injection systems rely on complex sequences where timing and pressure are prerequisites for ignition. A dead start after a rebuild often points not to a short circuit in the ECU wiring, but to a missing condition that prevents the control unit from commanding the injectors at all.

In the case of the 2012 Ford Fiesta 1.4 L TDCi (also known as the 1.4 HDi), the symptoms describedâzero voltage on the injector plugs and a hot ECU power relayâare classic indicators of a low-pressure safety interlock. The engine turns over smoothly with no weird noises, which rules out mechanical binding or catastrophic internal failure like a seized camshaft. This suggests the cranking system is functional, but the fuel delivery side has not met the minimum threshold required to enable high-pressure injection pulses.

The diagnostic data provided reveals a critical detail: the red wire on the injector plug shows 1.2 V while the black wire shows 0 V. In many modern diesel architectures, specifically those using Bosch-style common rail systems, the ECU monitors fuel pressure via a sensor in the high-pressure pump or the rail itself. Before applying the high-current pulse needed to open the injectors, the ECU checks this signal. If the system detects that the low-pressure pre-fill pump has not built up sufficient pressure, the ECU will logically withhold the injector command to prevent unburned fuel from flooding the cylinder, which could cause hydrolock or severe mechanical damage on a fresh rebuild.

The update confirms the root cause: the lack of fuel pressure in the rail meant the ECU refused to fire the injectors. Removing the fuel tank revealed an unusual configuration where the primary fuel pump was missing from its expected location near the filler neck, replaced only by the sender unit. This is a common point of failure in rebuilt engines if the aftermarket or remanufactured components are not sourced correctly. The manual priming method successfully built enough pressure to trigger the ECU's safety check, evidenced by the sudden appearance of 12 V on the injector lines and the onset of black smoke upon cranking.

The absence of strong suction during intake while using a jug suggests that either the low-pressure lift pump is inoperative or the filter is clogged with debris dislodged during the rebuild. On a diesel engine, air locks are particularly insidious; even a small amount of air trapped in the line between the tank and the high-pressure pump will prevent the system from reaching the ~30â40 bar required to start combustion.

The immediate next step involves verifying the integrity of the low-pressure fuel delivery path. If the original mechanical pump is indeed missing or non-functional, installing a new lift pump is mandatory before attempting another start with live batteries connected. Ensure that the manual priming tool is seated tightly on the filter head and that all connections from the tank to the high-pressure pump are leak-free.

There is also a nuance regarding the ECU power relay heating up during ignition. While this can indicate a grounding issue or excessive current draw, in this specific context, it likely reflects the ECU attempting to cycle its internal logic while sitting in a "limp mode" or waiting for the fuel pressure signal. Once the low-pressure pump is restored and the system is fully primed, that heat should subside as the ECU enters normal operating state.

For developers maintaining legacy automotive systems or working on custom builds, always remember that software logic gates (like the ECU's fuel check) will override hardware outputs if safety thresholds aren't met. Fixing the wiring or replacing the ECU won't help until the physical pre-conditionâfuel pressureâis satisfied.
